lines: Picture a batch run split into many identical slices, almost all of them healthy.
One slice happens to carry a record that breaks its worker every single time it's tried.
With one shared allowance for failures across the whole run, that one broken slice is enough to take every other slice down with it.
What would let that one broken slice fail on its own, without dragging the healthy ones down, and what does the run report once it's over?
Does giving each slice its own failure allowance change whether the run itself still counts as having failed?
answer: Giving each slice its own failure allowance does exactly that: the broken one keeps retrying and eventually gets marked failed on its own, while every healthy slice finishes untouched.
But the overall run still reports itself as failed, even though nearly everything in it succeeded — one marked failure is enough.

lines: Each worker in a run like this is told its own position in the line, by the control plane itself, through more than one channel at once.
That position is the only coordination it needs: a worker holding position three always handles slice three. Nothing hands out work from a shared pile.
Here's a detail easy to miss: the control plane can start a worker's replacement the moment the old one looks like it's on its way out, before that old one has actually finished dying.
For one short window, two workers can both believe they hold the same position — so whatever that position's work actually does has to tolerate being done more than once.
Give each slice its own failure allowance, and a broken slice retries on its own account and eventually gets marked as such, without ever pausing the slices around it.
Every slice still gets its turn to run; only the final count of who made it and who didn't changes.
Left alone, every slice still runs even if most of them end up broken — the run simply reports more failures.
Put a ceiling on how many broken slices are tolerable, and crossing it stops the run early instead of letting the rest limp through.
A failure can be read two different ways depending on what actually caused it, and a run can be told to treat each way differently.
A worker that exits because its own code hit a real bug can be told to stop the whole run immediately, no more retries.
A worker that's removed only because the machine underneath it needed to be cleared can be told the opposite: don't count that one against the budget at all.
A worker partway through its slice gets forced off its machine for maintenance, not because of anything it did wrong.
Does that removal eat into the same failure allowance every other kind of failure draws from?
answer: Only if the run was explicitly told to treat that particular kind of removal as exempt. Nothing in the system assumes it on its own.
Leave that rule unwritten, and a maintenance-driven removal counts exactly like any other failure.

lines: Not every run needs every slice to finish before it's genuinely done.
A run can instead be told which slice, or how many slices, succeeding is enough — and the moment that's true, it stops the rest and calls itself finished.
One slice's success can be the whole answer, with the other slices never needing to matter at all.
A finished run can be set to clean itself up automatically after a short wait, pods and all, which is genuinely convenient.
It also means whatever those workers printed on their way out disappears with them, unless something copied it out first.
A scheduled run is still going when its next scheduled start arrives, and there are only three ways that collision can be handled.
Let the new one start anyway, right alongside the old. Skip the new one entirely and wait. Or stop the old one outright to make room.
Same overlap, three completely different outcomes, chosen ahead of time.
A scheduler that's been offline for a while comes back to find it's missed a great many of its own scheduled starts.
Past a certain number of misses, it stops trying to catch every single one up and simply gives up on the backlog, logging that it did.
A schedule that reliably kicks off a run is not the same thing as a system that understands how those runs relate to each other.

It has no sense of one run depending on another, no notion of catching up a stretch of missed history, and nothing that strings failures across runs into an alert. That's a different layer entirely, built on top.
Giving a workload the right numbers still says nothing about when it's supposed to stop.
A nightly run isn't meant to live forever like a service; it has to finish, and be retried carefully when it doesn't — which is exactly what the next piece builds on top of.
